title: Fantasy Variation Crash Course! | Caro-Kann | GM Naroditsky’s Top Theory Speedrun

moves.spoken: We have White against the Caro-Kann — the pawn to e4, met by c6.
The pawn to d4, taking the centre.
Black challenges with d5.
The pawn to f3 — the Fantasy Variation, my official recommendation: the most fun line against the Caro by a country mile.
Black takes on e4, giving up the centre.
We recapture on e4. Capturing there only makes sense in the context of one specific follow-up.
Giving up the centre only makes sense if Black immediately follows with an important move.
That move is the pawn to e5, opening a path for the queen to h4, where it would fork the king and the e4-pawn — one of the main Fantasy lines.

Against the pawn to e5 we don't take and don't play d5 — both allow the queen to h4 — instead the knight to f3, sacrificing d4 for quick development. But Black plays the knight to f6, a developing move that isn't the main line and invites e5, like a souped-up Alekhine. The knight to c3 would let Black revert with the pawn to e5, so we go the other way.
The pawn to e5 — if we mishandle this, the knight leaps to g4 threatening a fork on f2 and to win e5 back with interest, so e5 is near-automatic.

Black retreats the knight to d5. We've bitten off a big centre with only pawns, so the pawn to c4 is tempting but risky — pushing more pawns invites overextension. Still, c4 chases the annoying d5-knight, and Black's one central break is the pawn to c5; if we ever meet that with c3, the d5-knight becomes unassailable.
So the pawn to c4 — I flip-flopped, but it works, provided we follow up with accurate development.

Black retreats the knight to b6. The knight to b4 would be no danger — a3 chases it. And the pawn to c5 is simply met by d5, making our centre even more imposing while the c4-pawn stays protected by the bishop. This transposes toward the Four Pawns Alekhine, where you develop the queen's knight first — otherwise the bishop to g4 pins the king's knight.
So the knight to c3 — the most accurate, waiting for Black's bishop before committing the king's knight.
Black develops the bishop to f5 — exactly the cat-and-mouse we wanted, the bishop out first.
Now we can safely play the knight to f3.
Black plays the pawn to e6 — and still not threatening c5, because we always have d5 in response; that's why developing the knight to c3 promptly mattered.

The bishop to e2 — not d3, which would encourage the bishop to g4. Then we castle and bring the other bishop to e3 to solidify. The centre is our main industry; we check for the c5 break every single turn, since we need d5 to answer it — then the queen to d2, a rook to d1, even b3 Alekhine-style to reinforce c4.
Black develops the bishop to e7 — and it really does look like a Four Pawns Alekhine.
We castle — an inferior version of that Alekhine for Black.
Black castles. As White we have everything we could ask for.
We complete development with the bishop to e3 — the bishop to f4 was a viable alternative, but for now we overprotect d4, the linchpin of the whole structure, in Nimzowitsch's sense.

Black plays the pawn to a5, grabbing queenside space — but it loosens the b6-knight, so d5 gains appeal. We avoid a4, which would leave a hole on b4 for Black's knight; if the pawn reaches a3 we just play b3, a move we wanted anyway. So we keep improving flexibly and decide where the queen belongs.

The queen to e1 — heading for g3 and a kingside attack down the semi-open f-file. It allows c5, but Black is so poorly developed that the rook to d1 answers it, and d1 is a better home than the queen there, since the rook x-rays the black queen.
Black plays the knight to a6, rerouting — and we'll make that hard.
The pawn to a3 — no downside, and it locks the knight in place on a6.
Black plays the queen to c7. The c5 break is still serious, but after the rook to d1 we either push d5 or Black trades on d4 into a central massacre.
The rook to d1 — protect the centre before anything else.
Black plays the rook to d8. The c5 break still isn't a threat, because we can meet it with d5.

The queen to g3, completing the maneuver. Why is c5 and d5 bad for Black? The pawn travels to d6, forking the queen and bishop and trapping the e7-bishop. Players under 1800 struggle under strain, and Black is very cramped with a storm brewing on the kingside.

Black plays the rook to d7, preparing to double. Now the d6-square is a major weakness — it'd be a dream to plant a knight there, so we manoeuvre toward it with the knight to g5 or d2. The knight to g5 lets Black trade the important dark-squared bishop, but after the recapture we threaten the bishop to f6 and stop Black doubling.
So the knight to g5 — the more adventurous choice, packing a slightly bigger punch.
In a classical game I'd lean toward the knight to d2.
But the knight to g5 is intimidating to face — and we still have d5 against any c5. An adventure with the knight.
Black plays the rook to d8 — a lot of players would reflexively play h6 here. There's a juicy rook sacrifice available, but in time pressure we just complete the maneuver with the knight to e4.
The knight to e4, heading for d6. The knight to d6 looks like it drops a pawn, but at the end of the line the pawn to c5 forks the b6-knight and whatever sits on d6.
So the pawn to c5 first, establishing the stronghold before infiltrating d6 — and Black meets us head-on with the pawn to c5.

The tempting knight to f6 with check fails to the bishop taking f6 and the recapture, winning our queen, with a fork on d4 at the end. So instead the pawn to d5 — the move we've prepared all game. The point: the f5-bishop is loose, so if Black takes on d5, the rook takes f5.
Black plays the bishop takes e4, correctly — and we don't automatically recapture.

The pawn to d6 — a beautiful in-between move, shoving the pawn to fork the minor piece and the queen while the e4-bishop still hangs. It gets very dicey for Black; the bishop takes d6 is the only grandmaster-level try, meeting the recapture with the queen to c6.
Black finds the bishop takes d6. But after the queen to c6 we play the pawn takes e7, and Black can't recapture, because the d8-rook would hang with mate once the queen has left.
We recapture on d6. Black's defence is resilient, but we're winning anyway.
Black plays the rook takes d6 — the losing move.
The rook takes d6 loses; the queen to c6 would also have lost, but far more resiliently.
This loses on the spot to several moves — what's the simplest for White?
Just the knight takes e4 — always look for hanging pieces first. The knight to b5 is even stronger, but I want my bishop.
The knight to b5 wins the rook outright.
But I'll take the bishop — in a way it shows the strength of our whole strategy.
The knight to b5 is objectively better.
Still, I wanted the hanging bishop — and the recapture on d1 changes nothing; we just take back and convert the extra piece.
The knight to b5 wins the whole rook, not just the exchange — I stand corrected.
The knight to b5 wins the rook because there are three attackers on d6 — the queen can't hold it.
Black plays the knight to c8. The downside is that Black gets three pawns for the piece, so conversion won't be trivial.
My guess is the opponent forgot the queen was protected by the knight — c7-square tactics are easy to miss.
Like the famous Magnus one-move blunder, dropping a bishop to c7. Now we can play fancy or utilitarian chess.
Let's play utilitarian — the knight captures on d6, taking the rook, the no-calculation move that ends the game.

I regret grabbing the d4-pawn earlier — taking on e4 first and then d6 would have been cleaner. The knight takes e4 was sloppy: had Black recaptured on d1 correctly, the c4-pawn would fall, costing a third pawn for the piece and making conversion far from easy.

It's over. We can pre-move: after either capture on d6, the bishop to f4 pins, and Black simply dies on the d6-square. Notice Black's queenside knight has been out of the game the whole time — my coach's lesson, that it's incredibly hard to play a middlegame effectively down an idle piece.
Black plays the queen to e7. That knight on a6 was dead the entire game — the c5 break was a dead end with a pawn in the way.
The rook takes f7 — simple. It matters that our d1-rook is protected by the bishop; otherwise Black could take on f7 and then on d1 with check and recapture, winning material.
A nice, instructive game. For context: the Alekhine is the pawn to e4 met by the knight to f6 — a move Alekhine popularized in the early 1800s, a period rich with historical chess tangents.
